How does a fridge or freezer work?

It's a heat pump. When you compress a gas, it gets hot, and when you decompress a gas it gets cold, but the total amount of energy is always preserved. Also, heat tends to flow from warm things to cold things until everything is the same temperature. So a simple refrigeration method is to take warm air, compress it so it gets hot, transfer that heat to air outside the refrigerator, then decompress the air and blow it into the refrigerator. This effectively moves the heat from inside the refrigerator to outside the refrigerator.
This is also why you cant cool a room by leaving your fridge doors open. It will make even more heat than keeping the doors closed.
No. That process adds slightly to the ability, but the main effect is in changing the boiling temperature of the gas.

The best way to think about the process of refrigeration is energy density.

Hot things Have a higher energy density than cold thing.

If we take air that is warm and compress it (i.e., make it smaller) the energy remains the same but the energy density increases because its in a smaller volume. If you let this hotter, higher density air cool down back to its warm temperature the energy density has decreased. Finally, if you uncompress the air you can increase its volume and further reduce its energy density which reduces its temperature. This is roughly how a refrigerator works.

The main effect comes from changing the boiling temperature of a gas.

The cycle is as follows:

A refrigerant gas (there are hundreds of different such gases, the general process is the same for all of them save ammonia though) is compressed, this makes the gas very hot (it is not a 1:1 correlation like the ideal gas law suggests, because we aren't working with ideal gases, but increase the pressure and you increase the temperature), and raises the boiling temperature. The gas then passes to a condenser, the heat of the gas bleeds off (into the air for systems you're familiar with, though commercial refrigerators often dump the heat into a water pipe to be carried outdoors) and the gas condenses into a liquid.

Step two, the liquid passed through a pressure regulator, dropping the pressure, because the pressure drops the temperature drops as well and the boiling point drops.

The liquid then passes through an evaporator, where it absorbs a large amount of heat and boils. A fan passes air over the evaporator and the air passing over the evaporator drops to a temperature around 5-10C above the boiling temperature of the refrigerant. This makes the freezer cold, and deliberately weakened insulation between the freezer and refrigerator keeps the refrigerator at a 'high' temperature rather than have a second system (though high temperature systems that are only refrigerators exist as well that are almost identical, they'll use a different refrigerant and pressures).

The refrigerant, now a gas again, is passed back to the compressor.

The whole process is complicated in various ways by the need to ensure no liquid passes into the compressor, ensure that all oil returns to the compressor, refrigerants that are blends of different fluids, clearing ice off of the evaporator coil, storage of the refrigerant in off cycles. It can also be a lot more complicated (multi-compressor systems that deliver refrigerant to evaporators in rooms all over a house that was built without ductwork for example) But this is the general idea for almost all modern refrigerators and air conditioners, as well as some heating systems (that condenser coil is nice and toasty).
